topic: How do orbital configurations of LEO satellites impact beamforming design for minimizing path loss and maximizing coverage efficiency?
consensus_response: In LEO satellite systems, the high orbital velocities and dynamic network topology complicate beamforming design. Narrower beams can increase antenna gain but may also result in stronger inter-beam interference due to non-zero side lobes, increasing path loss and reducing coverage efficiency. To optimize beamforming, it is essential to balance these trade-offs while minimizing costs. Robust side lobe suppression techniques, adaptive beamforming algorithms, and clustering satellites into orbital planes can help mitigate the impact of high orbital velocities on the network topology, enabling better coverage and minimizing inter-beam interference. Furthermore, the use of high-frequency bands such as mmWave and THz can enhance data transmission speeds, but requires accurate and fast angle-of-arrival estimation to improve beamforming gain and radio link quality.
reference_context: The use of high-frequency bands like mmWave and THz can enhance data transmission speeds but require accurate angle-of-arrival (AoA) estimation to improve beamforming gain and radio link quality, especially in low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) regions. Massive MIMO and intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRS) can further improve coverage efficiency by increasing the number of antennas and controlling phase shifts, respectively.
